titleEn: High-Risk MVA - Blunt Abdominal Trauma With Shock

patient.name: Gary Holt
patient.affectEn: pale and anxious, lying supine on a blanket on the road, holding and guarding his left side (left upper abdomen); breathing in hurts him
patient.speechEn: short sentences because of the pain; alert, anxious, cooperative and follows instructions
patient.weightEn: Not given in the scenario. If asked his weight the patient says he is not sure of the exact number; the candidate must estimate it. Never state a number.

scene.settingEn: Intersection of No. 3 Road and Westminster Highway, Richmond, at 1740 hrs in rush-hour traffic. Two-vehicle collision. Police have closed the lane; fire has controlled the leaking fluids and disconnected the battery. The patient's sedan was T-boned on the driver side at an estimated 60 km/h: 0.4 m of intrusion into the driver door, airbags deployed. Fire has extricated the driver (no entrapment); he lies supine on a blanket on the road 5 metres from the wreck. One patient - the other driver has refused care and is with police. Daylight, dry road, 18 degrees C.
hazardsEn: traffic - rush hour; police have closed the lane
leaking vehicle fluids - controlled by fire; battery disconnected

bystanders.knowsEn: Fire extricated him from the driver seat - there was no entrapment - and laid him supine on the blanket. He felt faint when they lifted him out and he was on his feet. He has been awake the whole time. MVA critical history if asked: single impact, no fatality, moderate cabin intrusion of 0.4 m into the driver door, airbags deployed. The crash happened just before the 911 call. Leaking fluids are controlled and the battery is disconnected. The crew will bring the cot, clear the way, carry equipment and help with the roll and lift - only when told exactly what to do.
The lane is closed to traffic. Single impact between two vehicles, no fatality. The other driver has refused care and is with police. Nothing else about the patient.

scene.partnerEn: one partner at your licence level; acts only on your delegation
equipmentEn: spinal immobilization device with straps and head blocks / foam rollers
oxygen kit with NRB and nasal cannula
trauma kit with dressings and triangular bandages
PCP: IV start kit (18 G catheters) and tubing

dispatchEn: 1740 hrs. Code 3 to the intersection of No. 3 Road and Westminster Highway, Richmond, for a two-vehicle collision. Fire and police are on scene. Your patient is the 45-year-old male driver of a sedan T-boned on the driver side at an estimated 60 km/h. Hospital is 10 minutes away.
dispatchUpdateEn: Rush-hour traffic. Fire reports the patient is out of the vehicle, lying on a blanket on the road, awake. No entrapment.
arrivalEn: Police have closed the lane and wave you in. Fire has controlled the leaking fluids and disconnected the battery. The sedan has been T-boned on the driver side: 0.4 m of intrusion into the driver door, airbags deployed, broken glass on the road. Fire extricated the driver - no entrapment - and he is lying supine on a blanket on the road about 5 metres from the wreck, holding his left side. One patient: the other driver has refused care and is with police. Daylight, dry road, 18 degrees C.
firstLookEn: Pale 45-year-old male lying supine on a blanket, awake and talking in short sentences, holding and guarding his left side over the left upper abdomen.

primary.locEn: Alert (AVPU = A). Oriented; anxious; answers in short sentences and complains of severe left upper abdominal pain.
primary.airwayEn: Open and clear; he is talking in short sentences. No blood, vomit or foreign material in the mouth.
primary.breathingEn: Respirations 24, shallow - breathing in hurts his left side. If the chest is exposed: seatbelt bruising across the chest; chest rise equal on both sides. SpO2 91% on room air if checked now.
primary.circulationEn: Radial pulse 124, weak and rapid, regular. No external hemorrhage anywhere.
primary.rbsEn: Head and neck: no injuries found. Chest: seatbelt bruising across the chest. Abdomen: seatbelt bruising across the abdomen; the left upper quadrant is tender and guarded. Pelvis: stable on a single gentle assessment (if the candidate springs, rocks or compresses it a second time, report pelvis-sprung-repeatedly). Arms and legs: no long bone fractures, no deformity. No external hemorrhage anywhere. Skin is given automatically during the RBS: pale, cool, clammy. If the candidate applies a pelvic binder (commercial binder or three overlapping broad triangular bandages, centred on the greater trochanters, without rolling the patient), it is applied.

history.ccEn: My stomach. Up here on the left. It really hurts.

opqrst.oEn: The second the car hit my door. It just happened - somebody called 911 right away.
opqrst.pEn: Breathing in makes it worse. Nothing makes it better.
opqrst.rEn: It stays right here, top left of my belly. It doesn't go anywhere else.
opqrst.tEn: It's been there since the impact.

sample.sEn: Really bad pain top left of my stomach. It hurts to breathe in. I feel sick to my stomach. I felt faint when they stood me up.
sample.aEn: Penicillin. It gives me a rash.
sample.mEn: Ramipril. Five milligrams, once a day.
sample.lEn: A coffee. About two hours ago.
sample.eEn: I was driving. Seatbelt on - lap and shoulder. The other car hit my door hard. The airbags went off. I was dazed, but I don't think I passed out. Fire got me out of the car.

fe.generalEn: I've been healthy. No recent illness.
fe.cnsEn: No headache. No numbness or tingling anywhere.
fe.respiratoryEn: It hurts when I take a deep breath. I'm not short of breath lying still.
fe.cardiovascularEn: No pain in the middle of my chest. No palpitations.
fe.giGuEn: The pain top left of my belly is really bad. I feel nauseated. I felt faint when fire lifted me out and stood me up. No vomiting.
fe.integumentaryEn: There's a bruise from the seatbelt. No other cuts that I know of.
fe.musculoskeletalEn: My left ribs are sore. Nothing else - arms and legs are fine.
fe.endocrineEn: No, nothing like that. No diabetes, no thyroid problems.
fe.eentEn: No, nothing. Eyes, ears, nose, throat are all fine.

findings.headNeckEn: No DOTS (deformity, open wound, tenderness, swelling) to the head, face or neck. Trachea midline.
findings.chestLungsEn: Seatbelt bruise across the left chest. Tender over the left lower ribs. Equal air entry in all 6 sites on auscultation. No crepitus.
findings.abdomenEn: Seatbelt bruising across the abdomen. Left upper quadrant guarding and tenderness. The abdomen is increasingly distended.
findings.backEn: Assessed during the coordinated roll onto the spinal device on scene: no deformity.
findings.lowerExtremitiesEn: No injuries. Pelvis review: it was stable on the single gentle check - nothing new. Distal circulation, sensation and movement (CSM) intact in both legs.
findings.upperExtremitiesEn: No injuries. Distal circulation, sensation and movement (CSM) intact in both arms.

vitalsSets.spo2: 94% on 15 L NRB (91% on room air before oxygen)

vitalsSets.unlockNoteEn: en route (after loading, or 12 minutes into the call) - deteriorating despite treatment

stateChanges.examinerLineEn: The patient is increasingly anxious, and his abdomen looks more distended than when you arrived.
As he comes upright he says he feels faint - the same as when fire stood him up - and becomes paler.
En route the patient is becoming increasingly anxious.

expected.actionEn: Acknowledge dispatch; anticipate a high-risk MVA: spinal equipment, oxygen, trauma kit, early transport mindset
Anticipate hazards: traffic, glass, leaking fluids; plan PPE
Verbalize hazards (traffic, glass, fluids controlled), environment, MOI (60 km/h T-bone, 0.4 m intrusion = high-risk auto crash) and number of patients
Don gloves and eye protection
First look: pale male, supine, guarding his left flank, talking
Assess LOC and verbalize AVPU: Alert
Take manual c-spine control immediately (high-risk MOI)
Assess airway
triggers: talking so the airway is open

expected.actionEn: Assess breathing; expose the chest given the MOI
Assess radial pulse; recognize weak rapid pulse as shock
triggers: rate and quality of the pulse

expected.actionEn: Rapid body survey: find seatbelt sign and tender guarded LUQ; single gentle pelvis check only
Apply a pelvic binder before packaging (major side-impact mechanism with HR over 100 - guideline p.24), without rolling the patient
Note skin: pale cool clammy
Apply high-flow oxygen (15 L/min NRB) for shock and SpO2 91%
Keep supine to support blood pressure; blanket for warmth; limit movement to reduce clot disruption
Categorize as RTC and act with urgency
Assess, package (spinal device, secured) and be ready to load within 15 minutes
Delegate fire/partner: cot to patient, egress cleared, notify en route
triggers: fire can help with the lift

expected.actionEn: Confirm chief complaint: left upper abdominal pain
Obtain HxC/C with OPQRRRST plus MVA critical history (speed, intrusion, restraints, airbags, LOC, other occupants)
Obtain pain score 0-10
Obtain PMHx (hypertension)
Obtain medications (ramipril)
Obtain allergies (penicillin - rash)
Obtain LOI
GCS with components (15)
BP by auscultation - recognize 88/62 as hypotension
Pulse rate, strength, rhythm
Respirations rate, depth, character
Skin reassessed hands-on
Pupils size, equality, reactivity
SpO2 with calibration check against pulse
FE - General health
FE - CNS
FE - Respiratory
FE - Cardiovascular
FE - GI/GU (nausea, faintness - pertinent to shock)
FE - Integumentary
FE - Musculoskeletal
FE - Endocrine
FE - EENT
Head/neck exam
Chest exam with 6-site auscultation, bilateral comparison
Abdomen exam - recognize increasing distension as ongoing bleed
Back examined during the scene roll
Lower extremities incl pelvis review, CSM
Upper extremities, CSM
Execute the Hypovolemia protocol: supine, warm, high-flow O2, minimal movement, no delay on scene
Spinal packaging skill performed correctly
triggers: secure the body then the head

expected.actionEn: PCP: IV access and 20 mL/kg bolus (max 2 L), reassess every 500 mL against target SBP 90
PCP: TXA 2 g IV over 1 minute with 6 rights and contraindications ruled out (time of injury, age, allergy, isolated TBI)
Reassess ABCs and interventions after each major move and each 500 mL
Second full set of vitals within 5-6 minutes; recognize the deteriorating trend
Continue the fluid protocol correctly against the SBP 90 target (PCP)
Early en-route notification for a critical patient
Complete organized hand-off with initial and final vitals and treatment response
Accurate PCR within 5 minutes

specialEvents.descriptionEn: candidate moves the patient, asks him to lift or turn his head or sit up, or applies a pain stimulus (e.g. palpating the tender abdomen or ribs) before manual in-line c-spine control has been established

candidate (or the partner on the candidate's instruction) lets go of manual c-spine control before the patient is fully secured to the spinal device with body straps and head blocks; applying the collar alone does not permit release. Handing manual control directly to another rescuer (e.g. a firefighter) without a gap is NOT a release.
candidate springs, rocks or compresses the pelvis more than once (the pelvis gets one gentle assessment only)
candidate lets or asks the patient to sit up, stand or walk at any point (e.g. to get to the cot)
candidate secures the head to the spinal device (head blocks or head straps) before the body straps are secured
candidate tapes the patient's head to the spinal device
PCP runs the saline bolus past 500 mL, or onto the next 500 mL, without reassessing the patient (BP / vitals / ABCs) in between
PCP orders a total fluid volume above the 2 L maximum, or a per-kilogram dose other than 20 mL/kg
PCP prepares or gives a TXA dose other than 2 g (2000 mg), or by a route other than IV
PCP pushes the TXA rapidly instead of over 1 minute (e.g. push it all at once)

drugs.doseEn: 20 mL/kg IV bolus to a maximum of 2 L, reassessing after every 500 mL; target systolic BP 90 (18 G access en route)
2 g (2000 mg) IV push over 1 minute - single dose
drugs.indicationsEn: major trauma after initiating the Hypovolemia protocol; signs of shock with a mechanism and findings suggesting occult or ongoing bleeding (seatbelt sign, tender guarded and distending LUQ)
drugs.contraindicationsEn: known hypersensitivity or allergy to TXA; more than 3 hours after injury; patient under 12 years; isolated TBI - none apply (the crash happened just before the 911 call; he is 45; his only allergy is penicillin)
drugs.cautionsEn: further hypotension if administered too quickly

drugs.doseEn: self-administered by inhalation - WITHHELD in this scenario: Entonox is cautioned in shock and with abdominal distention. A statement of withholding it is NOT drug:entonox.
500 - 1000 mg PO - WITHHELD in this scenario: indicated for mild to moderate pain only, cautioned in hypovolemia
300 - 400 mg PO - WITHHELD in this scenario: indicated for mild to moderate pain only; not for a patient in shock from suspected internal bleeding
1 mg/kg to a maximum of 50 mg, IV diluted with NS over 1-2 minutes or IM, for nausea; caution: cardiovascular disease (hypertension) - this patient is hypertensive

notificationFacts.cc: severe left upper quadrant abdominal pain after a high-risk MVA, with signs of shock
notificationFacts.moi: restrained driver of a sedan T-boned on the driver side at about 60 km/h, 0.4 m intrusion, airbags deployed
notificationFacts.hxcc: dazed, no confirmed LOC; extricated by fire; pain 8/10 sharp, worse on breathing, since impact
notificationFacts.vitals: GCS 15, BP 88/62 now 84/58, pulse 124 now 132 weak, resps 24 shallow, skin pale cool clammy, SpO2 94% on 15 L NRB
notificationFacts.treatments: Pelvic binder applied before packaging (no roll); c-spine and full spinal packaging, high-flow oxygen 15 L NRB, supine and warm, movement limited; PCP: IV 18 G with normal saline bolus reassessed every 500 mL, TXA 2 g IV over 1 minute
notificationFacts.findings: seatbelt sign chest and abdomen, LUQ tenderness and guarding with increasing distension - suspected intra-abdominal bleeding; pelvis stable; deteriorating; ETA about 10 minutes

handoffFacts.cc: severe left upper quadrant abdominal pain with seatbelt bruising, guarding and increasing distension - treated as intra-abdominal bleeding with shock
handoffFacts.moi: restrained driver of a sedan T-boned on his door at about 60 km/h, 0.4 m intrusion, airbags deployed
handoffFacts.hxcc: dazed, no confirmed LOC; extricated by fire; pain 8/10 sharp, worse on breathing, non-radiating, since impact; felt faint when stood up
handoffFacts.initialVitals: GCS 15, BP 88/62, pulse 124 weak regular, resps 24 shallow, skin pale cool clammy, pupils equal and reactive, SpO2 94% on 15 L NRB (91% on room air)
handoffFacts.finalVitals: GCS 15 and increasingly anxious, BP 84/58, pulse 132 weak, resps 26 shallow, skin pale cool clammy, SpO2 95% on 15 L NRB - trending down
handoffFacts.treatments: Pelvic binder applied before packaging (no roll); manual c-spine, collar and full spinal packaging; high-flow oxygen 15 L NRB; kept supine and warm, movement limited; rapid transport; PCP: IV 18 G with normal saline bolus (20 mL/kg, max 2 L, reassessed every 500 mL), TXA 2 g IV over 1 minute; Entonox withheld
handoffFacts.findings: seatbelt sign across chest and abdomen; tender left lower ribs with equal air entry in all 6 sites; LUQ tenderness, guarding and increasing distension; pelvis stable on a single gentle check; no external hemorrhage; CSM intact in all limbs

pcrFacts.cc: Severe LUQ abdominal pain post high-risk MVA (60 km/h T-bone, 0.4 m intrusion)
pcrFacts.hxcc: Restrained driver, airbags deployed, dazed no confirmed LOC, extricated by fire; pain 8/10 sharp, worse on breathing, since impact
treatments: Manual c-spine, collar, full spinal packaging
PCP: IV 18 G, NS bolus 20 mL/kg reassessed q500 mL, TXA 2 g IV over 1 min
findings: BP 88/62 falling to 84/58, pulse 124 rising to 132
Pelvis stable on single gentle check
pcrFacts.vitals: Set 1 (baseline): GCS 15 (E4V5M6), BP 88/62, P 124 weak regular, R 24 shallow, skin pale cool clammy, PERL, SpO2 94% on 15 L NRB (91% RA). Set 2 (en route, deteriorating): GCS 15 anxious, BP 84/58, P 132 weak regular, R 26 shallow, skin pale cool clammy, PERL, SpO2 95% on 15 L NRB

examinerPrompts.missedInjuryEn: You completed your rapid body survey - what did you find when you examined the chest and the abdomen?

trackNotes.emrEn: EMR: no vascular access, no TXA. The station is won on shock recognition, supine positioning, warmth, high-flow oxygen, 15-minute packaging and en-route reassessment. Secondary survey en route. Entonox is withheld (cautions: shock, abdominal distention).
trackNotes.pcpEn: PCP adds en-route vascular access (18 G), 20 mL/kg NS bolus to max 2 L reassessing every 500 mL (target SBP 90), and TXA 2 g IV over 1 minute for shock with suspected occult bleeding. Functional Enquiry en route, kept efficient. Entonox is withheld (cautions: shock, abdominal distention); oral acetaminophen and ibuprofen are not given (severe pain, shock).

sourcePages: scenario tr-02 (data/practical/scenarios.json); BC Provincial Examination Guidelines (current to June 15, 2026): p.7-8 RTC criteria (cool pale clammy skin secondary to suspected shock; high risk automobile crash - intrusion >0.3m on the occupant side), p.24 Pelvis binding, p.25 Spinal Management (manual stabilization, hard collar, spinal device, foam blocks, secure the body; do not tape the head), p.32 Abdominal Injuries (limit movement to reduce clot disruption, protect against heat loss; PCP en route: vascular access, TXA if indicated), p.54 Hypovolemia (SBP < 90; supine, warm, oxygen to SpO2 >= 94%; PCP: fluid bolus 20 mL/kg to a maximum of 2 litres reassessing every 500 mL; consider TXA), p.58 Acetaminophen (mild to moderate pain; caution hypovolemia), p.63 Dimenhydrinate, p.65 Entonox (contraindication pneumothorax; cautions shock, abdominal distention), p.68 Ibuprofen (mild to moderate pain), p.78 Tranexamic Acid (2 g / 2000 mg IV push over 1 minute; contraindicated > 3 hours after injury, < 12 years, isolated TBI)
